```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6,
                      fig.height = 4, warning = TRUE, message = TRUE)
library(NationalModelUng2009)
```

## What this package does

The package predicts the **gross merchantable volume** of a forest stand
(cubic metres of wood per hectare, m³/ha) using the national models of Ung et
al. (2009). A stand here is an even-aged group of trees in which one species
makes up at least 75 % of the basal area.

A prediction needs four inputs:

| Input | Meaning | Unit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `species` | The tree species | code, scientific name or common name |
| `age` | Age of the stand | years |
| `dd0` | Degree-days above 0 °C in one year | degree-days |
| `map` | Total precipitation in one year | mm |

`dd0` is the sum, over all days of a year, of the amount by which the daily
mean temperature is above 0 °C. It is **not** the same as `DD5` (degree-days
above 5 °C), and it is **not** the variable called `DD_0` in ClimateNA or
`climr`, which measures degree-days *below* 0 °C. Using either of those
instead gives a wrong answer without any error message.

This document follows one stand through six steps:

1. Describe the stand and its location.
2. Choose a model.
3. Obtain `dd0` and `map` for the location.
4. Run the prediction.
5. Read the warnings.
6. Test how much the answer depends on the climate values.

## Step 1. Describe the stand and its location

The example stand is a white spruce stand, 80 years old, in the boreal forest
of Saskatchewan.

```{r stand}
stand <- list(
  species = "white spruce",
  age     = 80,
  lon     = -105.5,   # decimal degrees; negative in western Canada
  lat     = 54.1,     # decimal degrees
  elev    = 500       # metres above sea level
)
```

The package supports 25 species. List them with `ung_species()`. This command
shows the spruces:

```{r species}
sp <- ung_species()
sp[grepl("spruce", sp$common, ignore.case = TRUE), ]
```

The `species` argument accepts any one of the three columns (`code`,
`scientific`, `common`). Capital letters do not matter.

## Step 2. Choose a model

The package contains two models. Both give volume.

* **Nat1** predicts dominant height, then basal area, and then calculates
  volume from those two values. Besides volume it returns height (`H_Nat1`)
  and basal area (`BA_Nat1`).
* **Nat2** predicts volume directly from age and climate. It returns volume
  only (`V_Nat2`).

This package does not choose between the models for you. The default,
`model = "both"`, returns both volumes so that you can compare them. If the
two volumes differ by more than 30 %, the package issues a warning (see
step 5). Use `model = "Nat1"` or `model = "Nat2"` when you need only one.

Choose Nat1 if you also need height or basal area. Otherwise, report both
volumes, or state which model you used.

## Step 3. Obtain `dd0` and `map` for the location

The models need `dd0` and `map` for the location. There are three ways to
obtain them. Choose one.

**Option A: `climr` (needs an internet connection).** The function
`ung_climate()` looks up the climate of a location with the `climr` package.
The first call downloads climate data, which can take several minutes.

```{r climate-climr, eval = FALSE}
# remotes::install_github("bcgov/climr")   # once, if climr is not installed
site <- ung_climate(lon = stand$lon, lat = stand$lat, elev = stand$elev)
```

**Option B: a local copy of ClimateNA or ClimateBC (no download).** Run the
program for the location and request a climate normal. The
`run_climatena()` function of the GYClimTransferCFS package does this and
returns a table. The function `ung_climate_from_climatena()` then converts the
table to `dd0` and `map`. The table must contain the annual variables `MAP`,
`DD18`, `DD_18` and `DD_0`. Use `run_climatebc()` instead for locations in
British Columbia.

```{r climate-climatena, eval = FALSE}
sites <- data.frame(id = "stand1", lat = stand$lat, long = stand$lon,
                    elev = stand$elev)
normals <- run_climatena(sites, period = "Normal_1981_2010.nrm",
                         base_year = 2000, climatena_dir = "C:/ClimateNA")
site <- ung_climate_from_climatena(normals, id = "id2")
```

**Option C: your own values.** Use values from another source. They must have
the definitions given at the top of this document.

This vignette does not run ClimateNA, because ClimateNA must be installed
separately. The next chunk instead holds the annual values that **ClimateNA
version 7.60 returned for this point** (1981–2010 normals, longitude −105.5,
latitude 54.1, elevation 500 m), copied from a real run. The chunk applies the
conversion of Option B to them. For your own site, replace the table with the
output of ClimateNA, or use Option A or C.

```{r site}
climatena_output <- data.frame(id2 = "stand1", MAP = 461,
                               DD18 = 48, DD_18 = 6467, DD_0 = 2043)
site <- ung_climate_from_climatena(climatena_output, id = "id2")
site
```

The values are inside the range of the data the models were fitted to for
white spruce (Check 1 in step 6 shows the ranges).

Four points about the climate values:

* **Derived `dd0`.** Neither `climr` nor ClimateNA provides degree-days above
  0 °C. Both options calculate `dd0` as `(DD18 - DD_18) + 365 × 18 + DD_0`.
  The result is an approximation, and its error has not been checked against
  the climate values used to fit the models.
* **Period.** Request a climate normal (a long-term average, such as
  1981–2010), not a single year. `ung_climate()` uses the 1981–2010 normals.
  The functions cannot check which period a ClimateNA table holds.
* **One value per stand.** Use one `dd0` and one `map` for each stand. Do not
  change them as the stand ages. The paper used one climate value per plot.
  The paper does not state the averaging period of those values, so report
  which period you used.
* **Same definitions.** Whatever the source, `dd0` must be degree-days above
  0 °C per year and `map` must be precipitation in mm per year.

## Step 4. Run the prediction

First, predict the volume at the age of the stand.

```{r predict}
result <- ung_volume(stand$species, age = stand$age,
                     dd0 = site$dd0, map = site$map)
result
```

The columns `H_Nat1` (m), `BA_Nat1` (m²/ha), `V_Nat1` (m³/ha) and `V_Nat2`
(m³/ha) are the predictions. The columns `species`, `age`, `dd0` and `map`
repeat the inputs. The species is shown as its code.

A warning appears above the result. It states that a change of 100
degree-days or 100 mm changes the Nat1 volume by more than 15 %. Step 5
explains this warning, and Check 2 in step 6 measures the change.

The package also draws a yield curve, which shows volume against age. Give
`age` a series of values:

```{r curve}
curve <- ung_volume(stand$species, age = seq(10, 150, by = 10),
                    dd0 = site$dd0, map = site$map, warn = FALSE)
plot(curve)
```

Here `warn = FALSE` hides the warnings, so that the next step can explain them
for one case. Without it, this call would issue the horizon warning described
in step 5, because the ages span more than 10 years. The models were designed
for increment predictions over intervals shorter than 10 years, so read the
curve with caution (see "Limits of the models"). You can also pass several
stands at once. Give vectors, or the columns of a data frame, for the inputs.
The result has one row per stand.

## Step 5. Read the warnings

`ung_volume()` checks each prediction and issues a warning when the result may
not be reliable. Each warning states how many rows it applies to. The warnings
have these meanings:

| Warning class | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `ung2009_warning_age` | The age is below 10 years, or outside the age range of the fitting data for the species. |
| `ung2009_warning_horizon` | One call predicts the same species and climate over ages that span more than 10 years, for example a yield curve. The models were designed for predictions over intervals shorter than 10 years. |
| `ung2009_warning_climate` | `dd0` or `map` is outside the range of the fitting data for the species. |
| `ung2009_warning_sensitivity` | A change of 100 degree-days or 100 mm changes the volume by more than 15 %. |
| `ung2009_warning_models` | The Nat1 and Nat2 volumes differ by more than 30 %. |
| `ung2009_warning_output` | The volume or basal area is larger than any value in the fitting data for the species. |
| `ung2009_warning_na` | An input is missing, so the prediction is `NA`. |

A warning does not mean the calculation failed. It means that you should
treat the result with more caution.

The following example uses three stands: a stand that is 8 years old, the
example stand, and the example stand in a very warm climate (`dd0` = 3500).
Five warnings appear. In the result, the first stand has almost no volume,
because it is very young. The volume of the third stand is far larger than any
volume in the fitting data for white spruce, so it is an extrapolation and
should not be used.

```{r warnings-demo}
ung_volume("white spruce", age = c(8, 80, 80),
           dd0 = c(site$dd0, site$dd0, 3500), map = site$map)
```

You can hide one class of warning and keep the others:

```{r silence, eval = FALSE}
withCallingHandlers(
  ung_volume("white spruce", age = 80, dd0 = site$dd0, map = site$map),
  ung2009_warning_sensitivity = function(w) invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
)
```

## Step 6. Test how much the answer depends on the climate values

The model responds strongly to `dd0` and `map`, and the climate values for a
location are uncertain. Three checks show how much this matters.

### Check 1. Is the climate inside the range of the fitting data?

The table `ung_envelope` holds the minimum, maximum, mean and standard
deviation of each variable in the data used to fit the models, for each
species.

```{r envelope}
env <- ung_envelope[ung_envelope$species == "PICE.GLA", ]
data.frame(
  variable = c("dd0", "map", "age"),
  site     = c(site$dd0, site$map, stand$age),
  minimum  = c(env$dd0_min, env$map_min, env$age_min),
  maximum  = c(env$dd0_max, env$map_max, env$age_max)
)
```

A site value outside its minimum and maximum means that the prediction is an
extrapolation.

### Check 2. Sensitivity to small changes in climate

`ung_sensitivity()` repeats the prediction with `dd0` and `map` each raised
and lowered by 100 (degree-days and mm), and reports the largest percentage
change in volume.

```{r sensitivity}
ung_sensitivity(stand$species, age = stand$age, dd0 = site$dd0, map = site$map)
```

The columns `dd0_change_pct` and `map_change_pct` give the largest change in
volume, in percent, for a change of 100 in that variable. The column
`max_change_pct` is the larger of the two. A value above 15 triggers the
sensitivity warning. In this example, the Nat1 value is above 15 and the Nat2
value is below 15. You can change the size of the perturbation with the
arguments `d_dd0` and `d_map`.

### Check 3. A range of volumes from climate uncertainty

`ung_uncertainty()` draws many (`dd0`, `map`) pairs around your climate
values, predicts the volume for each pair, and reports a central interval.
The argument `seed` makes the result repeatable.

```{r uncertainty}
fan <- ung_uncertainty(stand$species, age = seq(20, 150, by = 10),
                       dd0 = site$dd0, map = site$map,
                       n = 500, seed = 1, warn = FALSE)
fan[fan$age %in% c(40, 80, 120), c("age", "model", "volume", "lower", "upper")]
plot(fan)
```

The column `volume` is the prediction at your climate values. The columns
`lower` and `upper` bound the middle 90 % of the predictions from the drawn
climate values. In this example the interval is wide, which agrees with the
sensitivity result in Check 2: small differences in climate change the volume
by a large amount.

Read the result with these points in mind:

* By default the spread of the climate values is the among-plot standard
  deviation of the species in the fitting data. It describes how climate
  differs from one location to another. It does not describe the error of
  your climate source. If you know that error, give it with `sd_dd0`
  (degree-days) and `sd_map` (mm).
* Only the uncertainty in climate is included. The uncertainty in the model
  parameters and the plot-to-plot variation of the real stands are not
  included. The interval is therefore **not** a prediction interval for the
  volume of a real stand.
* The column `prop_outside` gives the proportion of draws whose climate is
  outside the range of the fitting data. A large proportion means that much of
  the interval is extrapolation.

### Optional: a typical stand without site climate

If you omit `dd0` and `map`, the package does not ask for a location. The
authors fitted the model for each species to measured field plots, and each of
those plots has a `dd0` and a `map`. For each species, the package uses the
**average** `dd0` and the **average** `map` of that species' fitting plots. It
prints a message that says so. The averages are in the table `ung_envelope`
(columns `dd0_mean` and `map_mean`). They differ between species, so the two
species below are predicted under two different climates, which the result
shows in its `dd0` and `map` columns.

```{r defaults}
typical <- ung_volume(c("white spruce", "black spruce"), age = 80)
typical[, c("species", "age", "dd0", "map", "V_Nat1", "V_Nat2")]
```

This is useful for comparing species. It is **not** a prediction for a
particular site, because it uses the average climate where each species was
measured, not the climate of your stand. The usual warnings still apply, so the
sensitivity and model-difference warnings can appear here.

## Summary of the steps

1. Record the species, the age, and the longitude, latitude and elevation.
2. Decide whether you need Nat1 (height, basal area and volume), Nat2
   (volume only), or both.
3. Obtain `dd0` (degree-days above 0 °C) and `map` (mm) with `ung_climate()`,
   with `ung_climate_from_climatena()` (local ClimateNA or ClimateBC), or from
   your own source. Report the source and the period.
4. Run `ung_volume()`.
5. Read every warning, and decide whether the result is acceptable.
6. Compare the climate with `ung_envelope`, run `ung_sensitivity()`, and run
   `ung_uncertainty()`.

## Limits of the models

These limits are stated by the authors of the paper.

* The authors state: "the models developed here were designed for increment
  predictions over very short (< 10 years) intervals, as requested within the
  context of the CNFI. The absence of safeguards, such as an empirical
  adjustment to the number of merchantable stems per hectare, means that the
  user who may want to use these models for longer-term projections should use
  caution." (CNFI is the Canadian National Forest Inventory.) A yield curve
  over many decades is a longer-term projection in this sense. Treat the
  curve as an illustration of the fitted equations, not as a forecast for a
  stand.
* The models were fitted to temporary plots measured once, in stands where one
  species has at least 75 % of the basal area. For mixed stands, apply the
  model to each species separately.
* The climate terms describe the present relationship between climate and
  volume. Do not enter future climate projections to estimate the effect of
  climate change.

## Reference

Ung, C.-H., Bernier, P.Y., Guo, X.J. and Lambert, M.-C. 2009. A simple growth
and yield model for assessing changes in standing volume across Canada's
forests. The Forestry Chronicle 85(1): 57–64. <https://doi.org/10.5558/tfc85057-1>
